articles.title: In 1960, Pat Boone paid $159,000 for a 1939 Beverly Hills estate, later adding a guest house and turning an open-air patio into a rec room; 66 years later, the 1.12-acre home is asking $22.95 million
articles.summary: Six decades after singer and actor Pat Boone and his late wife Shirley bought a Beverly Hills estate for $159,000, the longtime family home has returned
articles.body: Six decades after singer and actor Pat Boone and his late wife Shirley bought a Beverly Hills estate for $159,000, the longtime family home has returned to the market with a $22.95 million asking price. The property at 904 North Beverly Drive sits on 1.12 acres in the Beverly Hills Flats and includes a 1939-built residence spanning 7,032 square feet. The listing describes the estate as a rare legacy property, with expansive lawns, mature trees and privacy despite its location near some of Beverly Hills’ busiest streets.Boone, now 92, has owned the property for 66 years. He bought it with Shirley in 1960 when the couple had four young daughters and were looking for a large family home. At the time, Boone was already a major recording artist and was starring in the television variety program “The Pat Boone Chevy Showroom.” The house was intended to give the growing family space to settle down, and its large lot was one of the features that attracted them.“When we found this place, it wasn’t my first choice because it’s at the corner of Beverly Drive and Sunset Boulevard, but it was a big lot and a beautiful home with all the bedrooms and baths that we would need,” Boone told Mansion Global.From $159,000 to $22.95 millionThe difference between the couple’s 1960 purchase price and today’s asking price highlights the dramatic rise in Beverly Hills real estate values. Boone paid $159,000 for the property when the home was only about two decades old. The estate is now listed for $22.95 million, according to its current Realtor.com listing. That represents an asking price more than 140 times the original purchase price, although the comparison does not account for inflation, taxes, maintenance, renovations or other ownership costs.The current listing describes the property as a six-bedroom, eight-bathroom residence with a three-car garage, swimming pool and separate guest house. Realtor.com lists the lot at 1.12 acres, or about 48,800 square feet.The property also has a history that goes beyond its size and price. Boone and Shirley hosted a number of Hollywood figures there over the years. Elvis Presley, Boone’s contemporary in the music industry, visited the house, including for pool gatherings in the 1960s. Actor Gregory Peck reportedly held a fundraiser in the yard, while Boone also hosted Bible study gatherings attended by celebrities including Zsa Zsa Gabor.A home built around family lifeThe Boones made several changes to the property during their decades there. They added a one-bedroom, one-bathroom guest house and a shed. An open-air patio was later enclosed and transformed into a recreation room.The room features a large dining table, wet bar and pool table, which is included with the property. It connects the kitchen to the pool area, creating a space designed for entertaining and family gatherings.The main residence has six bedrooms and eight bathrooms according to the current listing. The primary suite includes two bathrooms and a dressing room that was used by Shirley until her death in 2019. Realtor.com currently lists eight full bathrooms, while the Mansion Global report described the home as having seven bathrooms, reflecting a discrepancy between the listing data and earlier reporting.The house retains several features associated with its traditional design, including hardwood and carpeted floors, three fireplaces and a formal living and dining area. Outside, the grounds include a lap-style swimming pool, broad lawns, mature landscaping and a circular driveway.Why the land mattersFor the Boones, the size of the property was a major attraction from the beginning.Boone grew up in Tennessee, as did Shirley, and he has said the couple wanted a home with plenty of green space rather than a property dominated by concrete. He later described the estate as an oasis in Beverly Hills.The property sits near the Beverly Hills Hotel and close to Rodeo Drive, but its high hedges and expansive grounds provide a degree of separation from the surrounding streets. Listing agent Lea Porter of The Beverly Hills Estates described the more-than-an-acre parcel as unusually large for the Beverly Hills Flats.The current listing also emphasises the estate's potential for renovation or redevelopment, describing it as a property that could either be preserved or transformed into a new luxury compound.Boone's decision to sell comes after more than six decades at the property. His wife Shirley died in 2019 after 65 years of marriage, and Boone continued living at the Beverly Hills home. He had previously tested the market in 2014, when the property was listed for $18.499 million, but that listing was eventually removed. It was also listed in 2021 at $21.888 million before being withdrawn. The latest listing, launched in June 2026, puts the asking price at $22.95 million.For Boone, however, the property represents more than a luxury estate. It was the home where he and Shirley raised their daughters, entertained friends and spent more than half a century of family life.“I don’t need a place this big, but I love it, and I still walk around and enjoy it all,” Boone told Mansion Global as he explained his decision to downsize. Now, after 66 years, the 1.12-acre Beverly Hills estate is waiting for a new owner.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: UP RERA clears 12 projects worth Rs 1,664 crore across six districts, including Lucknow, Ghaziabad & Hapur
articles.summary: For homebuyers in Uttar Pradesh, a new set of housing and commercial projects is set to expand the state's real estate pipeline, with developments ranging
articles.body: For homebuyers in Uttar Pradesh, a new set of housing and commercial projects is set to expand the state's real estate pipeline, with developments ranging from residential projects in Ghaziabad and Hapur to a large mixed-use project in Lucknow.The Uttar Pradesh Real Estate Regulatory Authority (UP RERA) has approved 12 new real estate projects across six districts, involving an estimated investment of Rs 1,663.85 crore, according to an official statement.The projects, cleared at UP RERA's 214th authority meeting chaired by its chairman Sanjay Bhoosreddy on Tuesday, will together comprise 3,090 residential and commercial units.Lucknow leads investment and unit countLucknow accounts for the largest share of the approvals, with four projects involving an estimated investment of Rs 609.35 crore and 1,972 units.The four projects include two residential developments, one commercial project and one mixed-use development, UP RERA said.Ghaziabad follows with three residential projects involving Rs 605.06 crore. These projects will comprise 574 residential units.Hapur has received approval for two residential projects with an estimated investment of Rs 123.45 crore and 192 units.The remaining three projects are spread across Ayodhya, Prayagraj and Kanpur.The Ayodhya project involves an estimated investment of Rs 72.61 crore and will comprise 85 residential units. In Prayagraj, a project worth Rs 51.66 crore will have 109 units, while the Kanpur project involves Rs 201.72 crore and will comprise 158 units.Authority stresses timely completionUP RERA said the newly approved projects are expected to boost construction activity and create opportunities in allied sectors, including construction materials, engineering and transport.For homebuyers, the authority said its focus would remain on compliance with the RERA Act, timely completion of projects and protection of their interests.Bhoosreddy said transparent and systematic development of the real estate sector, along with timely approval and monitoring of projects, remained a priority for the authority.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Trump pushes Russia-Ukraine ‘energy truce’: Can it work?
articles.summary: Talks of a possible halt in attacks on energy facilities come as strikes on such targets continue unabated.
articles.body:
A proposal by US President Donald Trump for an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine appeared to be gaining ground this week when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was “ready” to make an agreement.

Trump has blamed the Ukraine-Russia war for the current record rise in diesel prices in the United States, which has become a major issue as the country approaches midterm elections in November.

Trump and Zelenskyy met for 40 minutes on Tuesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York to discuss efforts to end Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.

In comments to reporters at the UN headquarters, Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt strikes on Russian energy facilities if Moscow stopped targeting Ukraine’s energy systems as well. “If they don’t want us to attack their diesel and refineries, we are ready – if they will not attack our energy system, our electricity, heating system, water supplies,” he said.

The Trump-Zelenskyy meeting comes as a barrage of attacks on energy facilities by both Russia and Ukraine continues unabated, raising questions over whether such a truce could indeed be reached – and whether it could hold.

Why are Russia and Ukraine targeting energy facilities in particular?

This year, Ukraine has massively expanded strikes on Russia’s oil industry, using long-range drones to strike refineries and other energy facilities at sites up to 3,000km (1,865 miles) from the Ukrainian border. The aim is to disrupt Russia’s energy industry , which it relies on to fund its war effort.

A September 20 attack forced the Moscow oil refinery, which processed about 230,000 barrels of crude a day in 2024, to halt crude processing, the Reuters news agency reported, citing industry sources. Also this month, Ukraine launched its deepest-ever attack into Russia, targeting two Arctic gas condensate facilities more than 3,000km (1,865 miles) from its border.

On Wednesday, Russia slammed ⁠jet-powered drones into two petrol stations and other sites in Kyiv, killing ⁠one and injuring at least seven people. Ukrainian oil company Ukrnafta said Russia had hit one of its petrol stations ⁠in the capital, the ⁠sixth such facility attacked in recent weeks.

Zelenskyy also warned in a post on Telegram on Tuesday that Russia was planning “a new massive attack” against his country.

A bilateral energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia would involve a mutual halt of attacks on all energy-related targets in each other’s countries. What remains unclear is whether both sides can agree on the preconditions for it being set in place.

The Kremlin previously welcomed the US proposal for an energy moratorium while also calling for such measures to be extended to Russian seaborne energy exports and sanctions.

On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said, “Both the US and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter.” But he also insisted that there could not possibly be any discussion of easing sanctions against Russia “when Ukrainians live every day under the threat of missile and drone attacks”.

This week, Trump expressed concern about the extensive damage done by Ukraine to Russia’s fuel-processing capacity, which he said is stoking diesel prices and “hurting the world”. On Sunday, he asked Ukraine to stop hitting Russian diesel refineries in particular.

But Trump’s intervention to halt Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy facilities appears to contradict his administration’s general approach to Russian energy.

This month, the US Congress passed a new bill that gives Trump sweeping powers to impose sanctions on Russia’s crude exports as well as steep tariffs on buyers of Russian energy.

Analysts say that Trump’s approval ratings have slumped to a record low at home, and he is now likely hoping an energy ceasefire could reduce petrol and diesel prices at US pumps ahead of the November midterm elections.

Furthermore, amid fears that Russia will try to cripple Ukraine’s heating and power facilities as winter approaches – as it did last year – Zelenskyy has asked Trump for additional Patriot air defence missiles, the only weapon in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of downing Russia’s ballistic missiles.

A halt to attacks on energy facilities, instead, would ease that pressure on Washington, whose supply of Patriots is being depleted by the US-Israel war on Iran.

But while such a ceasefire could lower prices, it would also likely aid Russia’s war economy, analysts said.

“The ongoing sales of Russian fossil fuels continue to finance Russia’s war against Ukraine,” Amanda Paul, senior policy analyst at the European Policy Centre (EPC), told Al Jazeera.

“Rather than putting the emphasis on the impact of Ukrainian strikes on fuel prices, Trump should be putting greater pressure on Russia to end its attacks and bring the war to an end,” she said. “Trump himself is responsible for stoking high energy prices, due to the repercussions of the US-Israel war on Iran and the subsequent blocking of the Strait of Hormuz .”

Marnie Howlett, an associate professor of international relations in Eastern Europe and Eurasia at the University of Oxford, said that by pressuring Zelenskyy, Trump was placing emphasis on the wrong actor in the war.

“It is Russia’s – not Ukraine’s – responsibility to end the attacks,” Howlett told Al Jazeera. “The Russian Federation has repeatedly broken ceasefire agreements, so the war will continue until it agrees to recognise Ukraine’s territorial sovereignty.”

Could Trump bring about an energy ceasefire?

Christopher Pool, a researcher at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, said Trump actually holds little leverage over the Ukrainian deep-strike campaign and has been “mysteriously reticent” to put pressure on Russia.

“A truce is more likely to be agreed because of pressures on both Ukraine and Russia caused by the war itself,” Pool told Al Jazeera.

“Ukraine is facing the hardest winter of the war, and memories of the brutal winter last year, when heating and electricity cuts were commonplace whilst temperatures dropped to minus 25 degrees Celsius [minus 13 degrees Fahrenheit], are fresh in Ukrainian minds.”

At the same time, Russia is facing its own energy crisis as a result of the Ukrainian deep-strike campaign. “The Kremlin may fear its effects on certain sections of the Russian population whose support, or apathy, is crucial for its survival,” the researcher added.

“The Ukrainian deep strike campaign therefore not only degrades Russia’s capacity to prosecute and escalate its war, but brings the war home to the very people the Kremlin is trying to shield from its effects.”

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, no ceasefires have been successfully maintained between the warring sides. During his presidential campaign in 2024, Trump claimed he would end the war in Ukraine very quickly if he resumed office as US president. However, this has not happened.

While Trump said last week that the two countries had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities, strikes resumed almost immediately.

In May, Trump announced a three-day ceasefire to mark ‌the end of World War II for the Russians. Russia announced a ceasefire for May 8 to 9 to coincide with commemorations of the Soviet Union’s victory over Nazi Germany, while Ukraine announced its own proposal for an open-ended ceasefire beginning on May 5.

But Moscow and Kyiv both quickly accused each other of violating these ceasefires. Talks deadlocked over ⁠Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, with Kyiv saying it would not pull troops back from parts of the region it controlled.

Ukrainian and Russian officials met in Turkiye for the first direct talks in years in May 2025, hoping to move forward on a full and unconditional ceasefire. The Istanbul talks resulted in an agreement to swap 1,000 prisoners of war each, but stopped short of the most urgent objective of halting the hostilities.

A previous round of talks in Istanbul in March 2022, soon after Russia invaded Ukraine, also failed to de-escalate the conflict and establish a diplomatic route.

Analysts say it is unlikely that a Trump-brokered energy ceasefire would be any different. “Russia is not interested in such a plan,” Paul said, as Moscow has been known to double down on attacks on energy facilities during the winter season.

“The Kremlin will exploit ambiguities in an energy truce by claiming that Ukraine violated the agreement and using that as justification for renewed attacks,” she said.

“Any deal would need clear rules, independent verification and a precise definition of what constitutes a violation – which will be hard to achieve.”

According to Pool, “Kyiv is likely to hold to its end of the bargain as long as Moscow does likewise.”

“Whether Russia does the same would be a reflection of how seriously the Kremlin takes the ongoing threat to the bubble in which urban and middle-class Russians have, to date, been able to live,” he said.

articles.title: Bilston venue The Robin angered by new Facebook subscription
articles.summary: The Robin in Bilston says it will not pay to be able to promote its events on Faceboook.
articles.body:
An independent music venue has said it will "absolutely not" pay for a new subscription service to promote its events on Facebook.

Meta, which owns the platform as well as Instagram, has started a new subscription called Meta One which limits the number of website links that can be posted - any more than two - unless a fee is paid.

Jack Heffernan, marketing manager for The Robin in Bilston, said the venue would have to pay £370 to keep posting as it currently does.

He said it would not be an issue for big businesses but really impacted smaller ones. The BBC has contacted Meta for a response.

The new subscription sets out various fee categories ranging from $15 [£11] a month to $500 [£376].

Heffernan said he was aware changes were being made by Meta and the idea had been "floated around" since December, but did not think they had been that transparent about it.

"We came in, began clearing up from the weekend, started scheduling some content and videos from the shows over the weekend and then all of a sudden 'you can't post this link'," he said.

"I thought 'oh, that's confusing?'. Looked into it and looked at the overall costs so I know what I'm dealing with, then when I came to see how much we would have to pay to post all of our links that we post... we'd have to pay for the largest package which is $500."

He said the move would affect lots of people and could "see it being the standard going forward", also impacting individuals in the future.

The venue would "absolutely not" pay the £370, he added.

"The average UK small business already pays between £500 to £3,000 per month of Facebook ads, so why should we then be forced to pay more?"

He said it was a case of "wait and see" what the impact on them would be as everybody "was in the same boat".

Matt Navarra, a social media analyst from Geekout Newsletter, said the fees were not yet universal, with subscriptions currently aimed at professional creators and businesses who get the option of posting links on Instagram, a new feature.

"But it is going to hurt smaller businesses - the likes of Coca Cola isn't going to be bothered about paying $300 or $400 a month whereas somebody who has got a corner shop or hair salon is going to feel the pinch."

He said Meta was testing whether being able to post more links makes its paid subscriptions more valuable, while also looking for new recurring revenue streams as it had been spending an "extraordinary amount" of money on AI "to keep up in the race to win the AI war" which amounted to almost $145bn so far.

Heffernan said the venue was well established and had a large following including other social media platforms, but Facebook and Instagram worked the best for its audience.

"It's quite a scramble for people to find out 'is there a way round it?" he added.

"Essentially they've taken out free features from the platform, including verification posts and links, and they're just selling it back to you."

articles.title: Sunny Hostin reveals she was holdout juror on case where man killed woman, dismembered her, boiled body parts
articles.summary: Sunny Hostin revealed she was the holdout juror in the 1991 Daniel Rakowitz dismemberment case, saying she saw clearly that he was psychotic.
articles.body: ABC'S "The View" co-host Sunny Hostin revealed on the liberal talk show Tuesday that she was a holdout juror on a case in a New York in the 1990s in which a man killed and dismembered his roommate, shocking her co-hosts as she argued, "I saw clearly that he was psychotic." As "The View" discussed the Lindsay Clancy case, Hostin said she felt that Clancy was not criminally responsible. She said she also felt strongly about the holdout juror because she was once a holdout juror. Daniel Rakowitz was found not criminally responsible by reason of mental disease or defect in 1991 after killing his roommate, Monika Beerle, with Hostin later identifying herself as the holdout juror who initially prevented the jury from returning a guilty verdict. Because the jury found Rakowitz "not mentally responsible" for the murder, according to The New York Times, he was sent to a state hospital in New York for the criminally insane. NBC New York reported in 2010 that Rakowitz would remain at the maximum-security Kirby Forensic Psychiatric Center on Wards Island after he petitioned to be moved. LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN Hostin, whose maiden name is Cummings and whose first name is Asunción, was quoted in a Feb. 23, 1991, New York Times report about the trial, which said, "Several jurors questioned afterward said one holdout juror was principally responsible for preventing them from returning a guilty verdict." "The View" co-host presented the article on the show while explaining the case. "That was me. It was because I saw clearly that he was psychotic," Hostin said Tuesday during the show. LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR ADMITTED 'REASONABLE DOUBT' BUT STILL REFUSED INSANITY VERDICT, FOREPERSON SAYS "'We don't think he intended to kill her,'" said a juror, Asuncion Cummings. "'But once he did, he dismembered her body in an effort to commit the perfect crime,'" the Times report read, quoting Hostin. "He did not mean to kill her, and once he killed her he panicked. He chopped up her body parts, yes, boiled her body parts, tried to commit the perfect crime," Hostin said during the show on Tuesday, noting how much she believed in the insanity defense as her co-hosts appeared shocked. "And he fed her body parts to the unhoused." LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR MAKES NEW PROMISE AS LAWYER WARNS OF PUBLIC ATTACKS Her co-hosts appeared shocked, as Alyssa Farah Griffin asked, "You got this guy off?" Hostin added, "All that being said it was so clear to me in the jury room — we were sequestered for nine days, one juror threw a chair at me. They were so angry at me. But one by one, I picked them off. What about this, what about that? We ended up, all 12 unanimously, voting that he was not criminally responsible by reason of insanity." The Times report from 1991 said Rakowitz, whom the report described as a "former mental patient," eventually admitted to boiling Beerle's body parts. He left her skull in the baggage room at the Port Authority Bus Terminal in New York City in a bucket of kitty litter. A witness, according to the Times, testified during the trial that Rakowitz had served soup to the homeless in Tompkins Square Park that contained a finger. When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, NewsBusters managing editor Curtis Houck said, "This is beyond parody. Absolutely breathtakingly stupid that she would not only admit to this but also act like it's a badge of honor." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Hostin brought the conversation back to the Clancy case and the news that Clancy's defense team was calling for an investigation into the holdout juror. Hostin called it "despicable." "The insanity defense is a real thing and I think this lawyer, you know, who is — wants the juror investigated. That’s going to have a chilling effect on juries. Jury duty is a duty. It is one of the most important things I think I’ve ever done in my life. It was extremely difficult but to investigate a juror for doing his or her duty is despicable," she said. Hostin went viral on Monday after she said her children faced racism while attending "predominantly White" private schools. Hostin brought up the topic while discussing 1619 Project founder and The New York Times Magazine reporter Nikole Hannah-Jones, who recently admitted she regretted aspects of her decision to send her daughter to predominantly Black, high-poverty public schools in Brooklyn in an effort to challenge educational inequality. "I think that this is a decision broadly that all parents make when it comes to educating their kids, but... this is a very difficult decision for Black parents, in particular, because I made a very different decision," Hostin said. "I sent my children to private schools, a predominantly White private school. So, while they didn't suffer academically, they excelled, but it was a well-funded school, a private school, well-resourced school, they suffered a different type of pain." "There was psychological trauma, there was racism that they experienced," she added. "They were bullied. There was, you know, trauma around their identity. My daughter wears a big afro, kids were trying to stick pencils in her hair. Boys were calling her butter face, meaning she looked good, but her face, and she is a beautiful girl." While Hostin conceded that her children "did not struggle academically" as Hannah-Jones' daughter reported, she expressed concerns about the "systemic problem" affecting predominantly non-White school districts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Media Research Center associate editor Nicholas Fondacaro told Fox News Digital on Tuesday that it was the latest example of Hostin viewing everything "from a prism of racism."

articles.title: Meet Khaos Kook, the 18-year-old Washington violinist whose concussion kept him from playing for over six months; he turned recovery into a protocol for injured musicians and won $25,000
articles.summary: Meet Khaos Kook, an 18-year-old violinist from Shoreline, Washington, whose concussion and seizure in 2024 kept him from playing for more than six months
articles.body: Meet Khaos Kook, an 18-year-old violinist from Shoreline, Washington, whose concussion and seizure in 2024 kept him from playing for more than six months and forced him to rethink what it means to be a musician. During his recovery, he turned his personal struggle into a structured, evidence-based return-to-instrument protocol for injured musicians, alongside a broader framework that defines musicianship through listening, research, teaching and advocacy as well as performance. For this work, he was named a 2026 Davidson Fellow and awarded a $25,000 scholarship, one of the most prestigious honours for students 18 and under in the United States, according to the Davidson Institute and local reporting.A head injury that changed everythingKhaos Kook had been playing violin for more than 14 years when a serious head injury and seizure upended his life in 2024. The concussion left him unable to practice or perform for over half a year and required a full year of medical leave from school. For someone whose identity had been tightly bound to daily practice, rehearsals and concerts, the sudden loss of access to his instrument was not just a physical setback but an existential crisis.In that period of forced stillness, Kook began asking a question that would become the core of his Davidson project: What makes someone a musician when they can no longer perform? He realised that classical music culture often equates musicianship with continuous physical performance and relentless practice, leaving little room for artists who are injured, disabled, aging or otherwise constrained. His own experience became a lens through which he examined this narrow definition and searched for a more inclusive model.Turning recovery into researchOver the next 16 months, Kook explored multiple pathways for staying connected to music without relying solely on playing. He immersed himself in score study, historical research, scientific inquiry and deep listening, while also engaging in teaching, advocacy and community work. He gradually reintroduced physical practice and performance as his health allowed, but he treated these as just one part of a broader artistic life rather than the sole measure of his identity.A key outcome of this process was the development of an original return-to-instrument protocol tailored to musicians recovering from traumatic brain injury. Existing concussion literature offers general guidance on returning to school, work and sport, but it lacks music-specific steps that account for the cognitive, sensory and motor demands of playing an instrument. Kook’s protocol fills that gap with an evidence-based, stepwise approach that helps musicians and their teachers navigate the transition from complete rest to structured practice and eventual performance.Challenging the performance-only modelKook’s project goes beyond medical recovery. It challenges the assumption that musicianship is defined only by the ability to perform on an instrument. He proposes a broader framework in which sustained artistic, intellectual and social engagement all count as legitimate forms of musical life. In this model, an injured violinist who cannot yet play can still be a musician by studying scores, researching repertoire history, writing about music, teaching theory, advocating for hearing health or organising community concerts.This perspective is particularly important for classical music, which often celebrates prodigious technical skill and continuous performance schedules. By widening the definition, Kook aims to make the field more welcoming to people who face physical or cognitive limitations at any stage of their careers. He argues that injured, disabled, aging or otherwise constrained musicians should not feel that their identity disappears when performance becomes difficult or impossible.From personal project to public resourceKook has already begun applying his philosophy in practice. He founded Project CliKK, a music nonprofit focused on expanding access to high-level music education. Through this organisation, he leads hearing health seminars and advocacy efforts, drawing on his own research experience with Dr. Sharon Kujawa at Mass Eye and Ear. These activities reflect his belief that musicians can have impact not only through concerts but also through research, education and public service.His return-to-instrument protocol is intended as a practical resource for other musicians and teachers facing similar challenges. By offering structured, music-specific guidance, it gives injured artists a clearer path back to their instruments while validating the work they can do in the meantime. In a field where recovery is often unstructured and isolating, such a protocol can provide both direction and reassurance.Recognition and next stepsIn 2026, Kook was named a Davidson Fellow in Music, receiving a $25,000 scholarship. The Davidson Institute, founded by Bob Davidson in 1999, recognises profoundly intelligent young people and supports them in developing their talents to make a positive difference. Kook is one of three Washington teens honoured that year, alongside Aditya Sengupta and Bryan Zhu of Bellevue, who together share $150,000 in scholarships.For Kook, the fellowship is more than financial support. It is affirmation that adversity can be transformed into a powerful source of inquiry. He has described the award as especially meaningful because his work emerged from a period when he felt cut off from classical music, an integral part of his identity for more than a decade. He has studied at international music institutes including Heifetz, Keshet Eilon and Mozarteum’s ISA, and has been invited to solo with six professional orchestras across the United States and Europe. He was also named a 2026 YoungArts Winner with Distinction in Classical Music and is a nationally recognised poet and essayist. His interests span English and music, with plans to continue exploring across disciplines in college.Outside of music and research, he enjoys off-piste skiing, cheering for Tottenham Hotspur and spending time with his Goldendoodle and Aussie Shepherd. These details paint a picture of a teenager whose life is rich and varied, even as he navigates the demands of high-level artistry and academic work. They also underscore his belief that a musician’s identity can be multifaceted, rooted in more than just hours of practice and stage time.Why this matters for young artistsKook’s story offers a model for other young musicians who face injury, illness or burnout. Instead of framing a break from performance as a failure or an end, he shows how it can become a period of growth, reflection and new kinds of contribution. His return-to-instrument protocol and broader framework provide language and structure for conversations that many students and teachers struggle to have.In a culture that often prizes constant productivity and visible achievement, Kook’s work is a reminder that rest, recovery and intellectual engagement are also part of a meaningful artistic life. articles.title: Bollywood actor Sumeet Singh Sarao faces garden bulldozing at £900,000 home after six-year council row over 1.4m raised ground; lived there with parents for 14 years, spent £8,000-£9,000 on garden
articles.summary: Bollywood actor and commercial singer Sumeet Singh Sarao is facing the prospect of having a large section of the garden at his £900,000 home in Telford,
articles.body: Bollywood actor and commercial singer Sumeet Singh Sarao is facing the prospect of having a large section of the garden at his £900,000 home in Telford, Shropshire, dug up or potentially bulldozed after a six-year planning dispute with the local council. Sarao, 39, has been locked in a battle with Telford and Wrekin Council since he raised part of his garden by around 1.4 metres during landscaping work in 2020, with the council arguing that the changes have caused an unacceptable loss of privacy for neighbouring residents.The actor, who has lived at the property with his parents for 14 years, says he spent between £8,000 and £9,000 on the garden and only raised the lower section to bring it level with the existing higher part of the plot. However, following enforcement proceedings, he has now been told to lower the garden to a depth of 1.6 metres at the end closest to the boundary, with the ground gradually sloping to around 900mm near the house. The dispute could ultimately result in the council carrying out the remedial work itself and recovering the costs from him.Sumeet Singh Sarao disputes council's privacy concernsSarao has rejected the suggestion that his landscaping work has resulted in significant overlooking of neighbouring properties. He says the garden boundary already has mature trees, bushes and a thick hedge that provide substantial screening."There is already a thick hedge along the boundary that prevents overlooking which is much taller than me - it just doesn't make sense," Sarao said, according to The Sun.He also claimed that both he and his neighbour would need a step-ladder to see over the existing fence.The actor said he has attempted to resolve the issue by offering additional landscaping measures, including replacing existing planting with a continuous row of conifers to strengthen the privacy screen. According to Sarao, however, the council rejected the proposal on the grounds that the planting would appear too bulky."I offered to replace the existing planting with a continuous row of conifers to create an even stronger privacy screen," he said."But the council rejected that proposal, saying it would appear too bulky regardless of me trying to co-operate."Actor says planning dispute has caused stress for his familySarao said the prolonged planning dispute has taken a toll on his family and left him feeling as though he is being treated unfairly."I'm just a normal human and don't cause any harm to anybody. It feels really unfair," he said.He added that he feels he has been "made out to be a criminal" over the garden alterations.The actor said he carried out the landscaping himself during the Covid period. Council planners subsequently contacted him and told him that he needed to seek retrospective planning permission for the changes.Sarao has maintained that the work was intended to level the garden rather than create an elevated area overlooking neighbouring homes.Council warns of further enforcement actionThe dispute has now escalated into formal planning enforcement proceedings. Telford & Wrekin Council maintains that the raised garden causes unacceptable harm to neighbouring residents through overlooking and loss of privacy.The council says it has a responsibility to uphold planning regulations and protect the amenity of neighbouring properties.An enforcement notice issued against the property was subsequently supported by an independent planning inspector following an appeal in September 2025.Under the requirements, Sarao has been instructed to excavate the garden to 1,600mm at the boundary end and create a slope towards the house, where the depth would be reduced to 900mm.Sumeet Singh Sarao proposes alternative solutionSarao insists he is not refusing to comply with the planning process. Instead, he says he has proposed an alternative solution that would involve removing the retaining wall, creating a sloping transition near the boundary and introducing substantial additional landscaping and screening."The council has now contacted me to arrange a meeting, although they have not indicated whether they are willing to consider any alternatives," he said."We are simply asking for fair treatment, proper engagement and a reasonable opportunity to agree a solution that protects neighbouring amenity while taking account of the practical circumstances at the property."He has also warned that physically excavating the garden could require walls to be removed to allow heavy machinery, including bulldozers, to access the site.Sarao said, "I've spent around £8,000 to £9,000 on the garden and put a lot of work into it.""If I don't comply, they could carry out the work themselves and charge me for the cost."Council says enforcement notice remains in forceA spokesperson for Telford & Wrekin Council said the matter has been subject to planning and enforcement investigations for several years.The council said it had subsequently considered a pre-application submission from the landowner in an effort to explore a revised scheme, but concluded that the proposal did not satisfactorily address the planning harm identified.The spokesperson said the enforcement notice was upheld by the Planning Inspectorate in September 2025, with additional time provided for compliance."Despite this, the required remedial works have still not been carried out and the site remains in breach of planning control," the council said.It added that it is considering further formal action, which could include prosecution proceedings or carrying out works in default and recovering the costs from the landowner.The council said its preference remains to secure voluntary compliance but argued that it must ultimately act to uphold the planning system and protect neighbouring residents.It has asked Sarao to provide a timetable for completing the required remedial work and has also offered to meet him in person to discuss a resolution.You use AI every day. articles.title: Man cautioned over Reform conference assaults in Birmingham
articles.summary: West Midlands Police is investigating a number of assaults after protests interrupted the Reform UK conference.
articles.body:
A man has been given a caution by police as part of an investigation into assaults on protesters at the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham earlier this month.

Footage appeared to show protesters being manhandled by audience members as they were thrown out. One woman had her hair pulled, and was was hit with a walking stick.

West Midlands Police said it was investigating assaults on five people and two other men had been voluntarily interviewed, as inquiries continued.

It said the man who was given a conditional caution had also volunteered for interview.

The force has asked alleged victims and anyone with information to come forward.

Activists disrupted the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, four times during his speech at the NEC on 4 September, before they were removed by security.

A West Midlands Police spokesperson said: "Our investigation into a number of assaults that took place at the Reform UK national conference at the NEC continues.

"One man has been given a conditional caution after being voluntarily interviewed as part of the investigation."

Cautions are offered by police if they have enough evidence to convict and the person involved has admitted their part in a crime.

Conditional cautions are the more severe of the two types of caution. Agreeing to a caution is an admission of guilt.

People who agree to conditional cautions can be subject to certain terms, which can include a fine, reparations to the victim or rehabilitation.

articles.title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.summary: Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison Wednesday, more than a year after a jury found the former Hollywood mogul guilty of sexually assaulting former “Project Runway” production assistant Miriam Haley in a high-stakes retrial.
articles.body: Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison Wednesday, more than a year after a jury found the former Hollywood mogul guilty of sexually assaulting former “Project Runway” production assistant Miriam Haley in a high-stakes retrial. Weinstein appeared in the downtown Manhattan courtroom in a wheelchair, his hands cuffed to his seat. In a victim impact statement read aloud in the courtroom, Haley said Weinstein “abused his position and power,” causing a “devastating effect on my life and security.” “It is a life sentence for me,” Haley said. Weinstein also addressed the court, again denying the allegations against him while apologizing to “anyone I may have hurt by my actions.” He had pleaded not guilty to a charge of first-degree criminal sexual act. “I am not a perfect person,” he said, “but I am a person who has made mistakes.” He later added: “I am not a violent man.” Judge Curtis Farber excoriated Weinstein before handing down his sentence. “You took what you wanted by force, and you have never accepted responsibility,” the judge told the former entertainment industry kingmaker. Farber said Weinstein’s 15-year sentence will be followed by five years of supervised release and a requirement that he register as a sex offender. Wednesday’s sentencing came after a protracted series of trials, appeals and courtroom proceedings that have kept Weinstein behind bars since his arrest in 2018, one of the key events of the #MeToo movement. Six-year legal odyssey Weinstein was originally convicted in 2020 of third-degree rape involving former aspiring actor Jessica Mann and first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley. He was sentenced to 23 years in prison. But his conviction was overturned in 2024 by a New York state appeals court, and a judge ordered a new trial. Weinstein was again found guilty in June 2025 of first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley, who testified that he forcibly performed oral sex on her in his New York City apartment in 2006. The same jury acquitted him of a separate criminal sex act charge involving allegations from former model Kaja Sokola. The jurors at Weinstein’s second New York trial could not reach a verdict on the charge related to Mann’s allegation, and a third trial on that charge also ended in a hung jury. In late June, prosecutors declined to try the Mann case a fourth time. Weinstein was separately convicted in Los Angeles in December 2022 of rape and two counts of sexual assault related to a 2013 assault of an Italian actor and model. He was sentenced by a Los Angeles judge to 16 years in prison in February 2023. He is set to be resentenced in L.A. after an appeals court vacated his original sentence. The former producer and film distributor vehemently denies all allegations of sexual misconduct, insisting his sexual encounters were consensual. In all, more than 80 women have accused Weinstein of sexual assault or harassment. Weinstein once lorded over Hollywood. Miramax, his first distribution label, released seminal independent films like “Clerks” and “Pulp Fiction.” He won an Oscar as a producer of “Shakespeare in Love.” In the early 2010s, his second distribution company scored back-to-back best picture wins for “The King’s Speech” and “The Artist.” But his reign came crashing down in 2017 after The New York Times and The New Yorker published exposés detailing his alleged pattern of sexual harassment and assault. The first wave of accusations against him in 2017 propelled the #MeToo movement, a reckoning with sexual misconduct by powerful people in high-profile professions. In recent years, Weinstein’s health has visibly declined, and he has faced various medical issues, including diagnoses of bone marrow cancer, kidney disease and diabetes. He has been held at the Bellevue Hospital prison ward, and he will remain there until he is sent to a state prison.

articles.title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
articles.summary: In court, Miriam Haley said the assault had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
articles.body:
Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.

In a victim impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".

Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".

Weinstein has already spent several years jailed in New York while he has faced three trials in New York over rape and abuse allegations. He has a separate conviction for sex crimes in Los Angeles.

This is the second time he has been given a prison sentence in the Miriam Haley case.

Weinstein was originally convicted and sentenced in the case in a 2020 trial, where he was also found guilty of raping actress Jessica Mann. But in 2024, New York's highest court overturned the convictions, ruling Weinstein did not get a fair trial.

He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.

Weinstein, 74, is currently being held in a prison ward at New York's Bellevue Hospital for a series of ailments reported during his incarceration.

Once the high-flying producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, Weinstein fell from grace after the New York Times and the New Yorker revealed multiple women's allegations of sexual assault stretching back decades.

The accusations against him sparked the #MeToo movement, but New York prosecutors have had to navigate a twisting path in securing convictions and sentences.

The 2020 trial was for charges involving Haley and Mann.

Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006.

"I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she told the BBC of her decision to testify.

In a retrial last year, the jury found him not guilty of sexually assaulting model Kaja Sokola.

No verdict was reached in two trials on a charge of rape related to Mann.

The jury could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg pursued another trial on that charge. In May, the jury in the retrial deadlocked and the judge declared a mistrial.

Meanwhile, Weinstein is awaiting a new sentence in California for his 2022 conviction of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in a hotel room in 2013.

An appeals court denied Weinstein's request to overturn the California conviction, but ordered a resentencing. It found the judge who gave Weinstein his original 16-year prison term had considered the New York convictions that were later thrown out in determining the sentence.

Weinstein has consistently denied the allegations against him, and has said in interviews he believes he will be proven innocent.

As he sentenced Weinstein to a decade and a half in prison on Wednesday, Judge Curtis Farber criticised the former Hollywood mogul's stance.

"You took what you wanted by force and you have never accepted responsibility," Farber said.

articles.title: Millions of heads of lettuce ruined by aphid outbreak
articles.summary: Growers are facing losses of £10m, as 30 million heads of lettuce will be rendered unusable.
articles.body:
Millions of lettuces are set to be wasted as farmers are grappling with a record outbreak of aphids that has devastated the end of their growing season.

Growers are facing losses of £10m, as 30 million heads of lettuce will be rendered unusable, according to the British Leafy Salads Association (BLSA).

The organisation says that warm and dry weather has produced "ideal conditions" for the bugs, with as much as 30% of the UK crop between now and the end of October set to be wasted.

Homegrown lettuce dominates the market in the summer and early autumn weeks before a transition that sees more imports filling shop shelves.

But imported lettuces are now likely to be on the shelves in the UK a couple of weeks earlier than usual.

Farms in many parts of England - the Midlands, East Anglia, the south-east, south and north-west - have been impacted by the outbreak.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, BLSA spokesman Dieter Lloyd described the issue as "serious", while not affecting all of the UK crop.

He said people have been eating salads from UK products "all summer" but added: "The issue though is serious, the aphids bloom in June and again in August/September."

"What we're talking about here is the loss of the crop over the course of the last couple of weeks and the couple of weeks ahead."

He said that "this is not all of the heads in the UK, but it's a significant percentage of it" and producers are "looking at not using 30 million heads of lettuce at the cost of £10m to the growers".

Over the course of the season, UK growers produce around half a billion heads of lettuce.

Asked if weather is a factor that has contributed to the issues, Lloyd said that short-term weather patterns and regional variations do have an impact.

"We had a problem with aphids last year, we've had a mild winter which traditionally might affect the aphid populations and then they do like warm weather."

The National Farmers' Union said that they are looking to support growers and researchers amid the outbreak.

Martin Emmett, the organisation's horticulture chairman, said: "This summer's warm and dry weather created a number of challenges for growers and the effects are still being felt, with rising levels of pests and disease now adding further pressure to farming businesses following an already difficult period.

"While growers are working hard to tackle record high numbers of aphids, the NFU is supporting the work of grower groups, plant breeders and researchers."

We have to start somewhere,” Zelenskyy said.The remarks came at Ukraine's Crimean Platform summit on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, ahead of a UN Security Council meeting on Russia's war in Ukraine.India has been pushing for dialogueThe reference to India's role comes amid New Delhi's efforts to remain engaged with both Moscow and Kyiv and encourage an end to the conflict.External affairs minister S Jaishankar said earlier this month that India had been in continuous touch with both Ukraine and Russia and was exploring ideas that could contribute to mitigating and eventually ending the war.“What we are trying to do is to see if there are ideas and suggestions which can be developed in some way in which they will contribute to the mitigation, ideally, the cessation of the conflict,” Jaishankar said during his visit to Warsaw.Jaishankar has also said India's position is that the conflict should end through dialogue and diplomacy.During his visit to Kyiv earlier this month, he met Zelenskyy and Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha, with discussions including possible approaches to ending the conflict.“If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there,” Jaishankar said in Kyiv.Black Sea shipping remains key concernAccording to Reuters, Zelenskyy said Egypt, India and Turkey had proposed options to restore safe navigation for merchant vessels in the Black Sea, where cargo movements have been severely disrupted by attacks on ships and port infrastructure by both sides.Ukraine has been seeking ceasefires covering attacks on energy infrastructure as well as shipping in the Black Sea. articles.title: Yemeni government in military and diplomatic push to reverse Houthi gains
articles.summary: Government claims battlefield advances as diplomats attempt to put anti-Houthi fight at UN centre stage.
articles.body:
The Yemeni government suffered a significant blow earlier this month when it lost the country’s Red Sea coast to the Houthi rebels. It is now working on a two-pronged strategy, militarily and diplomatically, to restore the initiative and prevent the Houthis from consolidating their gains and pushing further into government-held territory.

Saudi-backed government forces claimed on Tuesday to have seized the strategic Mount Qarafan in southern Taiz’s al-Shamayatayn district. The military reported killing five Iranian-allied Houthi fighters and injuring 20 others during the operation.

Pro-government Homeland Shield Forces, also known as the Quwat Dira’ al-Watan in Arabic, also thwarted a Houthi infiltration attempt on the Kahboub front , which overlooks the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait. Government forces also reported the capture of Mount Zalat, near Kahboub, on Tuesday.

The battles in the mountainous regions of southwestern Yemen are critical because of the commanding positions the peaks being fought over provide. Qarafan overlooks valleys linking southern Taiz with western coastal areas, as the Houthis attempt to encircle government-held areas in the governorate. Kahboub, meanwhile, is significant because Houthi forces have been attempting to secure the high ground overlooking Bab al-Mandab to prevent a government counterattack and expand the territory under their control.

The Houthis, meanwhile, have claimed Saudi Arabia has conducted air strikes in Taiz, al-Jawf, and Marib. Riyadh has not confirmed the strikes.

The humanitarian toll is mounting, with recent hostilities displacing approximately 132,000 people, including 75,000 in Taiz alone, according to the International Organization for Migration.

Meanwhile, at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Yemeni government officials are attempting to rally support for their push against the Houthis.

Presidential Leadership Council member Abdullah al-Alimi is leading Yemen’s delegation and will address the General Assembly later this week, but has already met US politicians.

Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba is also attending the world gathering, and called for the disarmament of non-state armed groups at a meeting on the General Assembly’s sidelines.

Other world leaders have included references to events in Yemen in their own addresses to the General Assembly.

Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani addressed the assembly, reaffirming support for UN efforts to reach a comprehensive political resolution. He emphasised that any settlement must be based on the outcomes of Yemen’s 2013-14 UN-facilitated national dialogue, in a manner that preserves Yemen’s unity, sovereignty, security, and stability.

Ireland also highlighted the crisis, expressing deep concern about the humanitarian situation and stressing that freedom of navigation must be protected in the Bab al-Mandab strait.

The Yemeni government is focusing its diplomatic efforts on impressing on other countries the dangers of Houthi control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, and the threat of more attacks against shipping in the region.

While the government has the support of Saudi Arabia, many other world powers are avoiding any involvement in the conflict, including the US. Washington is already entangled in a war with the Houthis’ primary ally, Iran.

The Yemeni government’s current military counterattacks against the Houthis therefore remain localised, rather than a larger campaign, analysts say.

Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst, told Al Jazeera that the government’s recent attacks are an attempt to shift the momentum.

“Partially and tactically, the Yemeni Armed Forces stopped part of the Houthi rush seeking to secure and stabilise expansion on the coast, and moved to limited counter-attacks in the Taiz-Lahj [region] … while regaining dominant heights and positions,” Jalal told Al Jazeera. “The government is gradually regaining the initiative, but it has not yet launched a broad military campaign to reclaim the coast and other areas.”

Jalal noted the significance of the geography being fought over.

“Taiz is considered a key to protecting Bab al-Mandab from the east and communication routes with Lahj and Aden; therefore, regaining its dominant southern and western heights prevents the Houthis from stabilising and securing coastal gains and expanding south,” Jalal added.

Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told Al Jazeera that reasserting control remains a severe challenge for government forces.

“It is impossible for the government to regain momentum unless it manages to reclaim Bab al-Mandab,” Al-Muslimi said, adding that he believes it is unlikely, despite the flat and open nature of the geography of the region, which would make it easier for air power to target the Houthis.

Al-Muslimi said that, for the Houthis, the battles in Taiz may not be about seeking full control of the governorate, but instead be a way of keeping the main battle away from their newly gained territories.

“In Taiz, in my opinion, the Houthis do not need to control it as long as they besiege it, and in reality, they will not try to control it because it is a burden more than an opportunity,” Al-Muslimi noted.

articles.title: FBI investigates apparent breach of its jobs website. Hackers claim to have sensitive employee data
articles.summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its jobs website as a criminal hacking group claimed to have accessed "very sensitive data" on nearly all agen...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its jobs website as a criminal hacking group claimed to have accessed "very sensitive data" on nearly all agents and job applicants.

"The FBI is aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating," the bureau said in a statement. The website, the main portal for prospective employees to learn about the FBI and initiate the application process, remained offline Wednesday morning.

A message that circulated online from a hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the hack.

The message, directed to FBI Director Kash Patel as well as the assistant director in the charge of the FBI's cyber division, said the hacking group had "compromised very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job."

The claims could not immediately be verified, and an FBI spokesperson declined to comment further. An email to an address associated with the organization was not immediately returned.

In its message, ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations in an FBI public service announcement from May that described the organization as a "cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion."

That announcement characterized ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims," commonly harass or threaten victims and "may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist."

ShinyHunters said in its message to the FBI that it was "offended" by those characterizations and demanded that the FBI remove those claims.

The FBI has been a common hacking target.

In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of Patel's and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade.

articles.title: Second man arrested in death of Mississippi woman Tasia Fortune
articles.summary: Jackson police have arrested a second man in the death of Tasia Fortune and obtained an arrest warrant for a third suspect.
articles.body: Jackson police have arrested a second man in the death of Tasia Fortune and obtained an arrest warrant for a third suspect. Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney announced the arrest during a Tuesday night city council meeting. NBC affiliate WLBT of Jackson identified the man as Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25. “What I can tell you is, today, we’ve taken another person into custody and charged them with homicide in this case,” Brackney said. The U.S. Marshals are assisting with the third warrant. Fortune, a Black woman, was found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned home in Mississippi in August. The case quickly made national headlines and raised concerns because of the state’s history of racially motivated violence and distrust of police handling of death investigations involving Black people. Over the decades, Mississippi has had more public lynchings than any other state, according to the NAACP, with 581 recorded between 1882 and 1968. Earlier this month, Jarques Ratliff, 51, was arrested and charged with murder in Fortune’s death. He was denied bond at a court hearing after pleading not guilty. Both Ratliff and Lloyd are Black. A motive and Fortune’s cause of death have not been released. Police said Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune but did not release further details. The Jackson Police Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. It’s unclear whether Lloyd has obtained an attorney. Brackney said Fortune was found “in a hanging position.” “And I need to stay with that language as we move this case forward so we do not do anything to jeopardize this case,” she said. The chief said detectives are pursuing additional warrants for other suspects. “I will guarantee there are actually more arrests to come in this incident,” she said.

articles.title: The best non-toxic cleaning products for Legos, plushies, stuffed animals and other toys
articles.summary: I talked to cleaning experts to find the best and safest cleaning products for cleaning toys, stuffed animals and more.
articles.body: Maintaining a clean home all the time is already a feat on its own, but it can be even harder when you have young children, particularly ones who have lots of toys. While cleaning rooms and doing laundry are a part of everyone’s routine, keeping toys like Legos, stuffed animals, electronics and dolls clean isn’t on everyone’s list of chores. To find the best way to clean toys — and the best products to use — I spoke to multiple cleaning professionals for their guidance and recommendations. “Different materials absolutely need different care,” says Becky Rapinchuk, founder of Clean Mama, a cleaning blog and product line. In other words, some toys only need a wipe down with mild soap, while others may have to go in the washing machine or require more care. Read more about the best methods for cleaning toys below. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best chemical-free cleaners for toys The products below are either direct recommendations from our experts or staff members, or are based on our previous coverage and/or are from brands we’ve tested. As someone who writes a lot about cleaning, I rarely ever write a story without recommending this product from Dawn. It’s one of my, and NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin’s, favorite affordable cleaning products, because it is mild, effective and has many uses. I use it all the time to clean my kitchen countertops as well as my refrigerator. And while it’s great for cleaning dishes, it’s also a powerful mild soap that you can use to clean the surface of plastic toys. You can spray this onto a damp cloth and use it to wipe dolls, dollhouses, building bricks and other toys with finished surfaces. Avoid using it directly on or around batteries and electrical parts on toys to avoid damage. Almost every cleaning expert I talked to recommends using microfiber towels with warm water and mild soap to clean plastic toys. They last longer than paper towels, are reusable and are machine washable in warm water. NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans uses these microfiber cloths and says that they’re durable and don’t get ruined after many uses or after several washes. If you plan on cleaning toys that haven’t been used in a while, they’re likely covered in dust, especially if they have fabric or upholstered surfaces. This duster kit includes one handle and five dusters to clean around your home, including those toys. I use these to clean things like my television, around the bedside table, baseboards and coffee tables. They work incredibly well and they do an excellent job of attaching to dust like a magnet, not just pushing the dust from one spot to another — I rarely ever have to go over the same surface more than once. Plus, it’s easy to replace the duster head, which you need to do after a while. I love Method’s lineup of plant-based, non-toxic cleaning products and body washes, since they’re effective but don’t have strong chemical smells. These multisurface wipes are similar. They’re alcohol-free and made from ingredients like corn and coconut, according to the brand. The wipes are also compostable and each container has 70 wipes. People who bought them say they enjoy the lime scent and say that the wipes don’t rip easily as you clean. For an unscented option that’s also safe on toys, skin and other surfaces, try Dreft’s All-Purpose Wipes. If you use either of these, just be sure to avoid electronic and battery compartments and wipe the toys with a damp cloth after. These laundry detergent pods are unscented so they’re perfect for people who are sensitive to strong smells or don’t want toys to have a soapy fragrance. The pods are made from biodegradable ingredients, so they’re safe to use on even delicate articles of clothing and machine-washable stuffed animals. There are 64 pods in each plastic-free container. This option is made for sensitive skin so the pods are fragrance free and they’re accepted by the National Eczema Association. While they’re great for general cleaning, you may have to take further steps or use another product to get rid of harsh stains. Since many stuffed animals and toys are machine washable, a washing machine bag such as this one is a great option for getting them clean while protecting any delicate parts or material. They’re large enough to fit stuffed toys like Squismallows and Jellycats, but they’re also suitable for several types of clothing. You can use them for silk clothing, satin bedding, knits, scarves and other delicates. They also have a zippered closure to keep the toys inside the bag while they roll around in the washer. How to clean plastic toys (building bricks, dolls and playsets) For most plastic toys without compartments for batteries or any other electronic features, simple is best. You can clean them with items you probably already have in your home, particularly in your kitchen. “Hard plastic toys like Lego sets, play kitchens, and doll houses can be wiped down with a damp cloth and mild dish soap, or soaked briefly in warm soapy water and rinsed well,” says Rapinchuk of Clean Mama. “Avoid bleach and harsh disinfectants on plastic toys, as they can degrade the plastic or leave toxic residues.” Additionally, you shouldn’t use alcohol-based cleaning products to clean toys made of finished wood since it can strip the finish. You should also use soft tools, such as a microfiber cloth, to clean plastic toys instead of abrasive scrubbers, sponges or scouring pads to prevent scratches. For cleaning small pieces, like Legos, for example, it might be easier to wash them all at once by cleaning them in a sink or bowl with warm water and mild soap, instead of wiping each one hand by hand. “You never want to lose a [Lego] down the drain, so just do yourself a favor and throw a strainer in the drain to catch any strays so they don’t get lost forever,” says Ryan Knoll, owner of cleaning company TidyCasa. Lastly, disinfectants and alcohol-based cleaners, including disinfectant wipes, can also accidentally remove paint from toys, so that’s another reason to avoid them. It’s ok to use multi-surface wipes to clean plastic toys as long as you rinse them off after and use non-toxic ones that are free of alcohol. How to clean electronic and battery-powered toys Toys with electronic features like wires or battery compartments are a little more complex to wash safely. It can be tricky to clean them thoroughly without causing them to break from water damage. It’s important to never submerge battery-operated toys, but outside of this, you simply have to use steps similar to cleaning plastic toys. “Turn them off and remove any batteries so there’s no electricity running through them,” says Knoll. Then you can use a cloth dampened with a small amount of water and mild dish soap to wipe the surface of the toys. “Be especially careful around the battery components, speakers, charging ports, anything like that. You really don’t want any water inside.” How to clean stuffed animals Probably one of the most popular toy categories, stuffed animals aren’t always easy to clean if you want to avoid damaging them. Both Rapinchuk and Knoll recommend referring to a stuffed animal’s care instructions first to see the best way to clean it. In general, though, Rapinchuk says that it’s fine to machine wash many stuffed animals (unless the label says otherwise), but it’s important to wash them with cold water on a delicate cycle and with mild detergent. They recommend putting them in a pillowcase or mesh bag, like the Tenn Well Mesh Washing Bag. Rapinchuk and Knoll recommend against putting stuffed animals in a dryer, even if they’re machine washable, since the heat can damage them and cause pieces to fall off. “Machine agitation can damage sewn-on eyes, noses, or other features,”she says. “High-heat drying can warp, shrink, or melt synthetic fabrics or embellishments. Some stuffing clumps when wet and doesn’t fluff back up evenly. For delicate or vintage stuffed animals, hand-washing and air-drying is safer.” How I picked the best chemical-free cleaners for toys Below is everything I considered when making the list of cleaning products above, including guidance from our experts. Ingredients: Both Rapinchuk and Knoll recommend using the most mild options when it comes to soaps and detergents for cleaning most types of toys. Our experts say to avoid alcohol-based cleaning products and disinfectants, since they have harsh ingredients and the residue they leave behind would need to be rinsed off thoroughly. Additionally, alcohol in cleaning products can damage plastic surfaces, strip paint and damage the finish of some toys. With this in mind, I made sure to include cleaning products that are free of bleach, alcohol and other harsh ingredients. Scratch-free supplies: In terms of cleaning supplies, our experts’ advice was similar — they advise against using abrasive scrubbing devices, like sponges and scouring pads, and even microscopic foam scrubbers because they can be too tough for the surfaces of some toys. Instead, they recommend using milder physical cleaners, including microfiber cloths, which don’t leave streaks and are less likely to scratch surfaces. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. We did not ask her for product recommendations. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a commerce editor at NBC Selected, where I write about home, kitchen and cleaning appliances. I’ve written about how to clean stainless steel appliances, air fryers, hardwood floors and washing machines. For this story, I talked to multiple cleaning experts to find the best methods and products for cleaning toys. articles.title: September full Moon 2026: When to see the Harvest Moon
articles.summary: September's full Moon will rise across on Saturday 26 September. The best viewing conditions currently look to be across southern and eastern parts of the UK.
articles.body:
September's full Moon will be visible in UK skies this weekend, just days after the autumn equinox.

Known as the Harvest Moon, it will reach its fullest point at 17:49 BST on Saturday 26 September.

At that time it will still be below the horizon for much of the UK, but it will rise shortly afterwards and appear almost completely full throughout Saturday evening.

It gets its name from being the full Moon closest to the autumn equinox, which this year took place on Wednesday.

September's full Moon is traditionally associated with the harvest, because historically, the additional moonlight after sunset was useful to farmers gathering crops.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich also lists the Corn Moon as another common name, reflecting the crops traditionally harvested around this time of year.

However, it does not always fall in September and if October's full Moon is closer to the autumn equinox, it takes the title instead.

If you catch the Moon as it rises it may appear yellow, orange or even reddish.

This is not a special feature of the Harvest Moon, but simply that when it lies low in the sky and is close to the horizon, its light has to travel through more of the Earth's atmosphere before reaching our eyes.

More of the shorter blue wavelengths of light are scattered, allowing the yellows, oranges and reds to become more prominent.

Will the weather be clear enough to see it?

The current forecast suggests Saturday could bring some drier and brighter weather, particularly across parts of England. However, there is some cloud further west and rain for parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the evening.

The best chance of clearer skies currently looks to be across some southern and eastern parts of the UK, while conditions are expected to be more changeable elsewhere.

The exact times of the moonrise will vary across the UK but will be shortly after it reaches its fullest point.

Keep up to date with the weather where you are online or on the BBC Weather app.

articles.title: Syria’s al-Sharaa warns Israeli attacks endanger delicate post-war recovery
articles.summary: President Ahmed al-Sharaa calls for Israeli withdrawal, condemning its attacks as Syria emerges from civil war.
articles.body:
Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa has called for Israel to withdraw from internationally-recognised Syrian territory in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly, saying Israel’s actions undermined the country’s security and progress after a devastating civil war.

“We reject Israeli attempts to impose a fait accompli. We reject their aggressions, which undermine peace and security,” he said, asserting that there have been “500 air strikes, more than 1,200 incursions and 300 detentions” in Syria by Israel.

“It is reminiscent of [an] era that we thought was long gone,” he added.

Al-Sharaa, a former fighter aligned with Syria’s al-Nusra Front armed group, came to power in 2024 after overthrowing Bashar al-Assad’s regime.

Now charged with rebuilding the shattered nation, al-Sharaa told the UN that Syria had emerged “from crisis to an opportunity”.

“The bloodshed was stopped; destruction was stopped. Syria started the journey of reconstruction, of recovery,” al-Sharaa said, citing state control over arms, the lifting of international sanctions and the rebuilding of military and civilian institutions.

In a speech lasting about 10 minutes, al-Sharaa also cited the “safe and decent” return of about 3.5 million refugees and displaced people, after the conflict spurred a refugee crisis that strained neighbouring countries and stoked persistent hostilities towards migrants in some Western countries.

This was the Syrian president’s second address to the UN General Assembly following his speech last year.

Long an international pariah, Syria under its new leadership is now courting international investment and political backing even as its United States-backed neighbour, Israel, deepens ties with armed factions from Syria’s Druze minority.

Al-Sharaa urged the international community to commit to a 1974 agreement that created a UN-supervised separation zone between Israeli and Syrian forces, demanding that Israel withdraw from the occupied Golan Heights.

In July, during the first visit by a UN chief to Damascus since 2009, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reiterated that the area was Syrian territory, describing Israel’s occupation as “totally unacceptable”.

Al-Sharaa insisted the strategic and water-rich area “will remain Syrian territory” after Colombia recognised Israel’s claim of sovereignty over the area last month.
